arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Timothy Bishop argued the law violates the Commerce Clause. He stated it conditions sales on out-of-state farming methods. He claimed there is no valid safety reason for the ban.
Michael Mongan argued the law bars in-state sales. He said voters chose to pay higher prices. He asserted the Commerce Clause allows this local market choice.
Brian Kneedler argued the sales ban imposes a substantial burden. He stated it serves no legitimate local public interest. He claimed it acts as a trade barrier based on out-of-state conduct.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests whether a state can ban the sale of goods produced elsewhere under different standards. The dispute centers on California's Proposition 12. It restricts pork sales based on how animals were raised. Producers say this burdens interstate trade. The state says it protects local consumer preferences.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Pork producers want the Court to strike down the sales ban. They argue it forces out-of-state farms to follow California rules. This burdens interstate commerce without a valid local safety interest.
California wants the Court to uphold the law. It argues voters chose to pay higher prices. They wanted to refuse a market for meat they view as morally objectionable.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Producers argue the law is an extraterritorial regulation. It conditions sales on out-of-state farms adopting California methods. They claim this violates the Commerce Clause almost per se.
California argues the law only bars in-state sales. It does not regulate out-of-state production. The Commerce Clause does not prohibit voters from choosing ethical products.

paragraphs: Justice Kagan asked if a state forces out-of-state actors to comply. She questioned whether the state's market effectively mandates specific practices.
Justice Thomas asked if California could ban houses built with out-of-state wood. He explored whether product standards exclude foreign materials.

paragraphs: This case defines the limits of state power over interstate trade. It determines if states can ban goods based on out-of-state production methods. The outcome shapes how states regulate agricultural products. It impacts the balance between local values and national markets.
